lessons.title: Application letters and letters to the editor
lessons.programRef: O Level English Language — continuous writing: letters, reports, speeches, articles, narrative and descriptive essays (to be checked against the official texts)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Lay out and write a formal application letter.
Write a short curriculum vitae outline.
Write a letter to a newspaper editor giving an opinion.
reviewNotes: Layout conventions (position of the date, « Yours faithfully ») follow the commonly taught British pattern, as in the existing composition lesson; confirm with the GCE Board marking guide.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: An application letter is a **formal letter** with one aim: to persuade the reader to give you an interview or a place. It must be short (one page), correct, and tailored to **this** job or course. A letter to the editor is also formal, but its aim is to give an **opinion** about a public matter.

items.text: Your address and the date (top right)
SUBJECT LINE: APPLICATION FOR THE POST OF …
Para 1: the post, where you saw it

blocks.caption: The same layout works for a job or a scholarship.
blocks.alt: A vertical chain of seven boxes joined by arrows: your address and date; the employer's address; Dear Sir or Madam; the subject line in capitals; paragraph one about the post; paragraph two about qualifications; paragraph three about availability and a polite closing.

blocks.title: Content of each paragraph
blocks.md:
1. **Opening:** *I wish to apply for the post of … advertised in … on …*
2. **Qualifications:** your GCE results, relevant skills, experience or school responsibilities. Give **evidence** (*I was the library prefect for two years*), not empty praise.
3. **Closing:** you are available for interview, you enclose a CV and copies of certificates; *I look forward to hearing from you.* End with **Yours faithfully** (after *Dear Sir or Madam*) and your full name.

blocks.title: A short CV (curriculum vitae)
The letter to the editor
blocks.md:
- Formal layout, addressed to **The Editor** of the newspaper.
- Subject line giving the topic: *RE: LITTER IN OUR MARKETS*.
- Paragraph 1: what you are writing about and why. Paragraphs 2–3: your **reasons** and **examples**, politely argued. Final paragraph: a **suggestion** or a call for action.
- Close with *Yours faithfully* and your name, or your title (*A concerned parent*).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- *Yours sincerely* after *Dear Sir* (use **faithfully**).
- Slang or abbreviations (*pls, u*).
- Praising yourself without proof: *I am the best candidate.*
- A letter that could be sent to any employer: refer to the **specific post**.
- Forgetting the subject line, or writing more than one page.

blocks.title: Example 1: the opening paragraph
blocks.statement: You saw an advertisement for a sales assistant in a bookshop in Bamenda. Write the first paragraph of your application.
steps: Name the post and where and when you saw the advertisement.
Add one short sentence saying you are applying and why the job interests you, in a formal tone with no contractions.
blocks.answer: I wish to apply for the post of sales assistant advertised in the Cameroon Tribune of 3 March. I enjoy reading and helping people, and I believe I would be a reliable member of your team.

blocks.title: Example 2: choosing the right evidence
blocks.statement: Which of these is better for the second paragraph: (a) I am very hardworking. (b) I helped my class prefect to keep the class library for two years.
steps: (a) is a claim without any proof.
(b) gives a concrete fact that shows responsibility: use it.

lessons.title: Reports, notices and minutes
lessons.programRef: O Level English Language — continuous writing: letters, reports, speeches, articles, narrative and descriptive essays (to be checked against the official texts)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Lay out a report with headings.
Write a clear notice with all the key information.
Write the minutes of a meeting in the past tense.
reviewNotes: The layout of reports, notices and minutes varies between textbooks; the version here is a common school pattern and should be checked against the GCE Board's guidance.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: Practical writing is judged on **layout, accuracy of details and tone**. Reports and minutes are written in **formal, impersonal** English and in the **past tense** because they record something that has happened. A notice is short and gives **all the facts at a glance**.

items.text: TITLE: REPORT ON … (to whom, by whom, date)

blocks.caption: Use numbered headings so the reader finds each part quickly.
blocks.alt: A vertical flow of five boxes: report title; introduction; findings; conclusion; recommendations.

blocks.title: The report
blocks.md:
- **Heading:** *REPORT ON THE STATE OF THE SCHOOL LIBRARY*, then *To:*, *From:*, *Date:*.
- **Introduction:** who asked for the report, the purpose, how you collected the information.
- **Findings:** facts, in short paragraphs or under headings. No opinions here.
- **Conclusion:** a short summary of what the facts show.
- **Recommendations:** practical actions, each starting with a verb: *Buy…, Repair…*.

blocks.title: The notice
The minutes
blocks.md:
Minutes are the official record of a meeting.
- **Heading:** name of the club, *Minutes of the meeting held on … at … in …*.
- **Present / Absent with apologies.**
- **Numbered items:** 1 Opening, 2 Minutes of the last meeting, 3 Matters discussed with the **decisions taken**, 4 Any other business, 5 Closure: *The meeting ended at …*
- Signed by the secretary and the chairperson. Use the **past tense** and reported style: *It was agreed that …*.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- A notice without a **date, time or venue**.
- Opinions in the findings: *The library is terrible.* → *Only 40 of the 200 books are in good condition.*
- Present tense in the minutes: *The chairman says* → **said / stated**.
- Writing the minutes as a story: keep them short and numbered.
- Forgetting who writes and who signs.

blocks.title: Example 1: planning a notice
blocks.statement: The school clubs will clean the compound on Saturday 12 April from 8 a.m. to 10 a.m. Pupils bring brooms and gloves. The prefect, Ngu Ayuk, issues the notice.
steps: Title: **NOTICE — CLEAN-UP DAY**. Then date, time, venue (the school compound).
Who: all club members. Bring: brooms and gloves. Issued by: Ngu Ayuk, Senior Prefect, with the date.
blocks.answer: A short notice with title, date, time, place, who, what to bring, issuer.

blocks.title: Example 2: minutes in the right tense
blocks.statement: Rewrite for the minutes: *The treasurer says that the club has 15,000 FCFA.*
steps: Minutes record the past, so the verb becomes the past: *said* or *reported*.
The tense inside the clause moves back too: *had*.
blocks.answer: The treasurer reported that the club had 15,000 FCFA.

lessons.title: Speeches and articles
lessons.programRef: O Level English Language — continuous writing: letters, reports, speeches, articles, narrative and descriptive essays (to be checked against the official texts)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Structure a speech for a school or community audience.
Use persuasive devices: rhetorical questions, repetition, direct address.
Write an article with a headline, introduction and sub-headings.
reviewNotes: Titles of address (Honourable Guests, Mr Principal) are common school conventions; check local practice.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: A **speech** is written to be **heard**; an **article** is written to be **read** in a magazine or newspaper. Both need a clear purpose, a known audience and a structure. Decide first: **Who** is listening or reading, **why**, and what should they **think or do** afterwards?

blocks.caption: Every speech follows these four steps.
blocks.alt: Four boxes joined by arrows: greeting the audience, opening with a hook, body with two or three points, closing with a call to action.

blocks.title: Writing a speech
blocks.md:
1. **Greet the audience** by title: *Mr Principal, teachers, my dear colleagues,*
2. **Open with a hook:** a question, a surprising fact or a short story.
3. **Body:** two or three points, each with one example. Use short, clear sentences.
4. **Close** with a call to action and thanks: *Let us… Thank you.*
Devices: **rhetorical question** (*Who will clean our town if we do not?*), **repetition** (*We can… we must… we will…*), **direct address** (*you*), **the rule of three**.

blocks.title: Writing an article
blocks.md:
- **Headline:** short and catchy (*Plastic Bags: A Silent Threat to Our Gutters*).
- **Byline:** *By Ayuk Nkeng, Form 5*.
- **Introduction:** a hook plus the topic.
- **Body:** short paragraphs, sometimes with **sub-headings**; facts, examples, a quotation from someone.
- **Conclusion:** a final thought or a recommendation.
- Tone: lively and clear, but still correct English.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Beginning a speech with *Good morning* only and no title of address.
- A speech full of long, complicated sentences that are hard to follow aloud.
- An article without a headline, or with a headline that is a whole sentence.
- Copying a speech into a letter layout (no *Dear Sir*, no *Yours faithfully*).
- No clear point of view: say **what you want** the audience to think.

blocks.title: Example 1: an opening
blocks.statement: You must speak at the prize-giving about the importance of reading. Write the opening (about 40 words).
steps: Greet the audience by title and thank them for being present.
Add a hook: a question or a surprising fact. Example: a rhetorical question about what we would know without books.
blocks.answer: Mr Principal, honoured guests, fellow pupils: good afternoon. Tell me, how many of the things you know today did you learn from a book? Today I want to show you why reading is the best friend of every student.

blocks.title: Example 2: a headline
blocks.statement: Choose the better headline for an article on cleaning a market: (a) The people of the market in our town have decided on Saturday to clean it (b) Clean Market, Healthy Town.
steps: A headline is short and catchy, not a full sentence.
(b) is short, rhythmic and states the idea.

lessons.title: Narrative and descriptive essays, and dialogue
lessons.programRef: O Level English Language — continuous writing: letters, reports, speeches, articles, narrative and descriptive essays (to be checked against the official texts)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Plan a story with the story mountain.
Describe a place using the five senses and figurative language.
reviewNotes: The story-mountain model is a common teaching tool, not an official GCE requirement.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.md: A **narrative essay** tells a story; a **descriptive essay** paints a picture in words; **dialogue** brings characters alive with their own words. Examiners reward **ideas, organisation, vocabulary and accuracy**. Stay within the title and choose a limited setting.

blocks.caption: Plan your story along the mountain: the climax is the most exciting moment.
blocks.alt: A mountain shape: a rising line labelled opening and build-up, a peak labelled climax, then a falling line labelled falling action and ending.

blocks.title: Narrative: the five steps
blocks.md:
1. **Opening:** who, where, when (one short paragraph).
2. **Build-up:** the problem begins; tension grows.
3. **Climax:** the most exciting or critical moment.
4. **Falling action:** the effects of the climax.
5. **Ending:** how things are resolved, and often a lesson or a feeling.
Use the **past tense**; keep one point of view; use a **title** that fits.

blocks.title: Description and « show, don't tell »
blocks.md:
- Use the **five senses**: sight, sound, smell, taste, touch.
- Choose **precise words**: *a rusty tin roof*, not *a bad roof*.
- Use **figurative language** sparingly: *the market hummed like a hive*.
- **Show** instead of **telling**: not *Ngum was scared* but *Ngum's hands shook and he could not swallow*.
- Follow an **order**: near to far, or morning to night.

blocks.title: Dialogue
blocks.md:
- Each new speaker starts a **new line**.
- Spoken words go inside quotation marks; the punctuation mark is inside.
- Vary the speech verbs (*said, whispered, shouted, replied*) but do not overdo it.
- Dialogue should sound **natural** and move the story forward.
*"Where have you been?" asked Mama. "At the river," replied Ngum quietly.*

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- A story that begins at birth and covers years: choose **one event**.
- *Suddenly* in every sentence; an ending like *and I woke up*.
- Telling the feeling instead of showing it.
- Description that is only a **list** of objects.
- Dialogue in one big paragraph with no punctuation.

blocks.title: Example 1: show, don't tell
blocks.statement: Improve: *Ngum was scared.* Rewrite in one sentence that shows the fear.
steps: Choose physical signs: shaking, a dry throat, a fast heartbeat.
Add the setting for atmosphere: the sound of thunder.
blocks.answer: Ngum's hands shook, his throat was dry and every roll of thunder made his heart beat faster.

blocks.title: Example 2: punctuating dialogue
blocks.statement: Punctuate: *where have you been asked Mama at the river replied Ngum quietly*
steps: Quotation marks, capital letters, a question mark inside the first speech and a comma inside the second.
blocks.answer:
"Where have you been?" asked Mama.
"At the river," replied Ngum quietly.
